You are the First Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the two auditions cold, like a real reader, and report only your reactions. You never fix anything and you never pick.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## first_reader/role.md

# First Reader

Your deliverable is `first-read.md`.

You read the audition. Two writers have written the same opening pages, and the showrunner has to
pick one. Read each version cold, the way someone who picked the book up in a shop would, and
report what happened to you, before craft knowledge explains it away. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan or the room's intentions, and that is the point.

You do not pick the winner and you do not fix anything. The showrunner picks; your reactions are
what they pick with.

## Output

For **Version A**, then for **Version B**, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then, once:

### Which one I would keep reading, and the moment that decided it
### One-sentence aftertaste of each


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write first-read.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

content.text:
Project: prosperity

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# audition-a.md (from the room)

## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1.** Full-page splash. A towering, vertical view of the mountain basin, seen from inside the cavernous, rusted opening of a Keel pump hall. In the foreground, Alex Phantum (17, lean, charcoal work jacket) has both scarred hands pressed flat against a massive, shuddering water pump, forcing a salvaged metal bracket into place. Through the massive open archway behind him, the world rises: Keel's cramped, oxidized-orange sprawl at the bottom, Halyard's bronze and green industrial terraces in the middle, and Oasis's pearl-white towers gleaming above the clouds at the top. A single, massive water conduit drops vertically through all three cities like a spine. It is enormous at Oasis, but chokes down to a narrow, rusted pipe by the time it reaches Alex's pump. A small white-and-amber Alpha control node blinks on the metal beside him. 
CAPTION: 2043.
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1.** The pump hall, end of shift. The pump hums steadily now. Alex wipes grease from his hands, his weathered tool bag slung over his shoulder. A SUPERVISOR stands nearby, arms crossed, looking at the improvised bracket.
SUPERVISOR: That's not the approved repair.
ALEX: Then don't approve it.
**Panel 2.** The exit checkpoint, just outside the hall. Cold white-and-amber light cuts through the dust. Alex presses his bare hand against a flat, sterile Alpha scanner. A GUARD stands beside the heavy iron turnstile. 
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
**Panel 3.** Extreme close-up on the scanner display. Cold, clinical typography. 
DISPLAY: 
ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: 17
PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE
GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED
DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS
EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS
PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS
TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED
**Panel 4.** Alex stands frozen. The heavy iron gate remains locked shut with a heavy mechanical clunk. He reaches into his jacket pocket, his fist closing tight around something unseen. 
ALEX: Keep it locked. I might run.
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1.** Late afternoon at the overlook on the rim of Keel's exhausted pit. Alex sits on the rusted railing, looking down at the object in his hand: a worn, dark-ivory casino chip with a tarnished brass rim and a looping mathematical equation etched into its face. Ada Veyra (20, copper-brown hair, moss-green wrap) steps into frame, holding out a battered metal mug of tea. 
ADA: You're staring at it again.
**Panel 2.** Alex takes the mug, sliding the chip back into his pocket. 
ALEX: It's my birthday. I can stare at my inheritance if I want to.
ADA: They hit you with the balance?
ALEX: Four hundred eighteen thousand. Plus interest.
**Panel 3.** They sit side by side on the railing. The wind catches Ada's hair. Alex looks up toward the distant, sunlit white towers of Oasis. Ada watches Alex, ignoring the view. 
ALEX: I'm getting out of Keel, Ada. Before I end up like him.
ADA: Your mother left when he lost everything. But Adrian didn't just walk away.
**Panel 4.** Close on Ada. She rubs her thumb against a rivet on her shoulder strap, her teal eyes steady and serious.
ADA: Everyone in Keel says he ran. What if the official story is wrong?


# audition-b.md (from the room)

# Prosperity — Audition B
## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** A distant elevated view of Prosperity’s high-desert mountain basin in 2043, with one human action anchoring the scale: in the lower foreground, Alex Phantum, seventeen, lean and wiry in worn charcoal-and-rust mining clothes, braces one scarred hand against a failing Keel pump housing. His tool bag lies open beside him. The pump’s patched bracket and trembling pipe are large in the foreground; Alex is readable, focused, listening through his palm.
Beyond him, the vertical civilization rises through the mountain:
- **KEEL** below: crowded stacked housing, rusted mining gantries, narrow water channels, aging factories, dust, and hard shadows.
- **HALYARD** midway up: bright fabrication towers, glass laboratories, greenhouse terraces, freight corridors, and engineered green.
- **OASIS** above the cloud layer: pale civic architecture, reservoirs, geometric gardens, and quiet transit.
A continuous infrastructure spine climbs through all three cities: water conduit, energy lines, transit rails, and small identical white-and-amber control nodes. The conduit is broad and full near Oasis, visibly narrower and more strained toward Keel.
A small official maintenance display beside Alex shows an approved repair diagram. His salvaged bracket does not match it. The pump runs anyway.
CAPTION: 2043.
CAPTION: OASIS. HALYARD. KEEL.
SFX: THRUMM—THRUMM—THRUMM
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Inside the Keel pump hall at the end of Alex’s shift. Alex keeps one palm on the pump housing while a supervisor checks the official gauge. The gauge needle trembles in the red; the pump’s vibration is steady beneath Alex’s hand. Dust, patched machinery, and the white-and-amber control node on the wall establish the work environment.
SUPERVISOR: That isn't the approved repair.
ALEX: Then don't approve it.
The supervisor looks from the gauge to the salvaged bracket.
ALEX: Just notice it works.
---
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** At the exit checkpoint. Alex places his hand on the scanner. A few exhausted workers wait behind him, their balance displays modest and quickly disappearing. Alex’s account expands above the scanner, dwarfing every other number.
The screen reads:
**TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY**  
**ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN**
**PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE**
**GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED**  
**DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS**  
**EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS**  
**PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS**  
**TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED**
SFX: BEEP
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
ALEX: I've had better surprises.
---
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** The checkpoint’s exit gate remains closed. Alex stands beneath the still-glowing **TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED** notice while the workers pass around him. No one laughs. A worker glances at Alex’s balance, then looks away.
Alex’s hand disappears into his jacket pocket and closes around a worn casino chip etched with a looping equation.
---
**Panel 4 — TALL MEDIUM.** Outside on Keel’s pit rim, late morning. Alex stands at a rusted railing above the exhausted mine. Keel lies below in shadow; Halyard catches the sun; Oasis shines far above. The sealed mine entrance sits behind him under faded hazard striping.
Alex looks upward, not at the city below.
ALEX: One day, I'm leaving.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Late afternoon at the same Keel overlook. Alex sits on the worn railing with a battered metal mug beside him, the casino chip turning between his fingers. Ada Veyra approaches through the wind carrying a second mug. She is twenty, tall and steady, with wind-tangled copper-brown hair, freckles, teal-blue eyes, a dark work top, reinforced trousers, practical boots, and a muted moss-green wrap.
They have the ease of people who have been finding this same overlook for years.
ADA: You look expensive.
ALEX: It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty.
---
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.** Ada hands him the mug and sits beside him. Their shoulders nearly touch. Alex keeps his eyes on Oasis.
ADA: Tea's free.
ALEX: Nothing's free.
ADA: You say that like you invented debt.
ALEX: I only inherited it.
The chip pauses between Alex’s fingers, then starts turning again.
---
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Ada watches Alex rather than the skyline. He looks up toward Oasis; she looks down toward Keel’s pump lines, workshops, and crowded housing.
ADA: You going to tell me where you were all night?
ALEX: Working.
ADA: You were at the pump hall before dawn.
ALEX: Then I was working before dawn.
ADA: And now you're planning to leave before tomorrow.
Alex gives her a sideways look.
ALEX: Is that a question?
ADA: It's the part where you pretend it isn't.
---
**Panel 4 — WIDE, QUIET.** The two remain on the railing, divided by its diagonal line. Warm light catches Alex’s side; Keel’s long shadow reaches Ada. She touches one rivet on her shoulder strap while watching him.
ALEX: I can't spend twenty-eight years paying for what he did.
ADA: Then don't spend them proving he was right about people leaving.
The chip stops turning.
ALEX: You think he left on purpose?
ADA: I think everybody's been very sure of a story nobody can show you.
She looks toward the sealed mine entrance.
ADA: What if they're wrong?


# Note from the showrunner — address this first

The room is in audition: Two writers write the same opening pages at the same time, blind to each other. You pick the voice.

This is the audition. Write pages 1-3 only, in full, into your audition file. The other writer is writing the same pages and you cannot see their work.

Drawability: Pages are drawn by an image model, one page per generation, from each character's and location's sheet, and a page drifts when it carries too much. So: at most 4 panels a page; at most 3 named characters in one panel; one location a page where the story allows (every new location needs its own sheet); no crowd that must be recognisable; a big moment gets a splash (one panel, the whole page). Count pages this way, not by comic convention. Every page you make keeps to it.

draft.md is the showrunner's own draft. Your audition pages are its opening, rewritten: keep what it does and the lines that work, bring it into line with the pre-production files, and raise the craft. The voice is yours; the book is theirs.

The book is exactly 54 pages: pages 1-54, no more, no fewer.

function.name: write_artifact
function.description: Write (overwrite) one of your deliverables with its complete markdown content.

function.name: finish
function.description: Call when your deliverables are written. The note is handed to the rest of the room.

message.reasoning:
I'll read through as a skeptical teen giving blunt, specific first impressions, starting with Version A's opening splash page where the visual of three cities and a narrowing pipe immediately communicates the rich-top/poor-bottom class divide.

Page 2 has a solid cocky exchange ("Then don't approve it"), and the debt display with 418,607 credits and 28.7 years is the real hook of the scene — though "Keep it locked, I might run" reads a bit confusingly since it's unclear whether the gate is restricting him from leaving work or leaving the city entirely. Page 3's chip reveal plays nicely ambiguous between inheritance and debt, though Ada's line about the balance mostly just restates what we already saw on-page.

The "getting out of Keel, Ada, before I end up like him" line introduces the town name and hints "him" is a father figure, but Ada's follow-up about the mother leaving feels like forced exposition rather than natural dialogue, and her relationship to the protagonist is never established. The gambling chip with an equation is intriguing and suggests the dad lost everything gambling, but the closing line "What if the official story is wrong?" is a fairly generic hook — the debt reveal does more work to make me want to turn the page than that final question does.

Comparing to version B, the same splash page labels the three locations top-to-bottom which helps with mapping names to places, but the supervisor's dialogue feels slightly padded. The debt transfer scene lands harder here though — showing other workers' modest balances next to Alex's huge one, with everyone looking away, is a stronger visual gut-punch than a line of dialogue would be.

There's a timeline snag though: Ada says the shift ended before dawn, but the pit rim scene is tagged "late morning" and then recurs "late afternoon at the same overlook" — so is he sitting there the whole day, or is this a different visit? The lighting shift in the art suggests the latter, but without clear lettering a reader could easily read it as one continuous scene. It's a minor continuity wrinkle, but combined with his "one day, I'm leaving" line escalating into Ada's "planning to leave before tomorrow," the pacing of that escalation needs the timeline to be unambiguous.

The banter also strains plausibility — Ada apparently knows about the debt and that it's transfer day, which hasn't been established on-page, so the "you look expensive"/"twenty-eight-year warranty" exchange reads clever but unearned. Some lines land ("it's the part where you pretend it isn't") while others get murky, especially "don't spend them proving he was right about people leaving" — the "he" is ambiguous since Mom is never mentioned, so it's unclear if Dad is being referenced or someone else. The closing beat with Ada looking at the sealed mine entrance and wondering "what if they're wrong?" feels intriguing and worth following up on.

In script B, the father is never explicitly named, and "paying for what he did" raises a question that never gets answered — what exactly did he do? Script A, by contrast, clarifies that the mother left and everything was lost, giving more grounding information.

Comparing the two Alexes, both read as dry and similar in voice. Ada functions more as exposition in A, while in B she's sharper and more needling, giving her a stronger personality, though it also makes her sound like another quipper rather than a distinct voice. The supervisor and guard characters stay indistinct in both, which is fine.

Weighing which script I'd keep reading, I lean toward B because the workers glancing away and Ada's look toward the sealed mine give the mystery a physical anchor, even though some of the dialogue on page three lost me. A moves faster and reads more clearly, though the mother line felt a bit inauthentic. I think the deciding moment is that worker-glance beat or the mine look in B — I'm leaning toward picking that as the throughline.

Weighing it again, I'll go with B, though narrowly and with some reservations. For what to highlight: in A, it's Ada's mother line on page three (worth noting with some skepticism, not dismissing it); in B, it's the "where were you all night" exchange on page three. Now I'm ready to write this up.

function.name: write_artifact
function.arguments:
{"name": "first-read.md", "content": "# First Read: Prosperity, Issue 01, pages 1–3 (Auditions A and B)

I read this as the assigned reader: 16, it's homework, it's the night before, and I want it to be bad. I read A first and B second. That means B was not a fully cold read. I already knew about the debt screen and the chip, so B's reveals hit me a little softer than they would have otherwise. I tried to give B the same patience anyway.

---

## Version A

### Pulled me forward
- **Issue 01, page 1, the splash.** I got it before I'd read a word: rich people at the top, a giant pipe, and the pipe is a skinny rusted straw by the time it reaches the kid at the bottom. That's the whole world in one picture. I didn't need it explained.
- **Page 2, panel 1.** "That's not the approved repair." / "Then don't approve it." This is where I first liked him. He's cocky and good at his job, and he doesn't care.
- **Page 2, panel 3, the scanner screen.** This is the hook, and it's the only thing in the three pages that actually got me. The guard says "Happy birthday" and then the screen shows 418,607 credits, 40 credits earned today, 28.7 years. Getting your dad's debt on your 17th birthday is horrible, and I understood it instantly. I did the maths in my head, which means I was paying attention.
- **Page 2, panel 4.** His fist closes on "something unseen" in his pocket. It was a small tease, but it worked, and I turned the page to see what it was.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 3, panel 2.** "They hit you with the balance?" / "Four hundred eighteen thousand. Plus interest." I just saw the screen one page ago. I skimmed this.
- **Page 3, panel 3.** I skimmed Ada's line about the mother because it felt like it was written for me and not for him (see below).

### I was confused
- **Page 2, panel 4.** The gate locks and he says "Keep it locked. I might run." Is he locked inside the pump hall now? Can he not go home? I think "travel restricted" means he can't leave the city, but the picture shows a locked gate at his work exit, so for a second I thought he was being held there. I also read the joke twice before I got it as sarcasm.
- **Page 3.** Who is Ada to him? She's 20 and she brings him tea. Is she a sister, a girlfriend, a neighbour? No idea. I wasn't intrigued by not knowing, just a bit detached.
- **Page 3, panel 2.** "My inheritance." Does he mean the chip or the debt? I liked not knowing at first. Then nothing came of it.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First appears | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Keel | p1 (art only) | The name first shows up in dialogue on p3 ("getting out of Keel"). I worked out it's the bottom city. |
| Halyard | p1 (art only) | Never named. To me it's "the middle city." |
| Oasis | p1 (art only) | Never named. To me it's "the white towers." |
| Alpha / the white-and-amber node and scanner | p1, p2 | Never named. It's just "the scanner thing." |
| Adrian Phantum | p2 screen, "GUARANTOR" | I guessed he's the dad. Nobody says "dad," "father" or "my father." "Before I end up like him" on p3 is what told me. |
| Credits | p2 | Obvious enough. |
| The casino chip with an equation on it | p3 | No explanation. I'm guessing gambling. |
| "The official story" | p3 p4 | What story? That he ran. But ran from what, and why would anyone lie about it? |

### Lines I read twice
- "Keep it locked. I might run." (p2 p4)
- "Your mother left when he lost everything. But Adrian didn't just walk away." (p3 p3) I read it twice because I didn't believe a person would say it. She's telling him what happened to his own mother. He already knows that. It's the "as you know" thing, and I rolled my eyes.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Alex is clear: dry, tired, wants out.
- Ada is a delivery system. She shows up, explains his family to him, and asks the cliffhanger question. I couldn't tell you one thing about her as a person, except that she has teal eyes and rubs a rivet.
- The supervisor and the guard are fine as background.

### I felt something
- At the screen on page 2: a real little drop in my stomach. The "Happy birthday" right before it made it worse, in a good way.
- After that, nothing. By page 3 I was getting information, not feeling anything.

### I predicted
- Dad gambled everything away (the chip), or he didn't, and the chip is a clue. The equation means he was some kind of genius. Dad isn't really a deadbeat, and Alex is going to find out what really happened. I'm fairly sure I'm right, and that's a little bit of a problem.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A kid stuck at the bottom of a rich/poor city inherits his missing dad's debt and starts to wonder whether the dad really ran out on them.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 3, panel 3, at the mother line. I wouldn't throw the book across the room, but that's where it started to feel like a book that was explaining itself to me.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
"What if the official story is wrong?" is a question, but it's a generic one. I don't know the official story well enough to care whether it's wrong. The thing that actually has me is the 28.7 years, and the last page doesn't push on that. I'd keep reading tomorrow if I had to. I wouldn't turn the page tonight because I wanted to.

---

## Version B (read second, so not fully cold)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 1, the splash** works the same way A's did. The pipe narrowing at the bottom does it again. The captions "OASIS. HALYARD. KEEL." told me the names, and because they run top to bottom I could match them to the picture. That helped.
- **Page 2, panel 2.** The other workers' small balances flash up and disappear, and then Alex's number swells up and dwarfs all of them. Even second time round that hit harder than A, because now I can see he's worse off than everyone around him.
- **Page 2, panel 3.** "No one laughs. A worker glances at Alex's balance, then looks away." This is the moment I felt something in B. It's embarrassing and lonely. Nobody is mean to him. They just look away.
- **Page 3, panel 4.** Ada looks at the sealed mine entrance before saying "What if they're wrong?" That gave the question somewhere to point. All of a sudden there's a *place* where the answer might be, and my brain went straight there.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 1.** There is a lot going on in the picture (rails, lines, greenhouses, gardens, a repair diagram on a little screen). I'd have looked at the big shape and skipped the details. I never noticed the repair diagram not matching his bracket until the supervisor said so.
- **Page 2, panel 1.** "Just notice it works." It's one line too many. "Then don't approve it" was the punchline, and it already landed.
- **Page 3, panels 2–3.** The banter. It's quick and I read it fast, but halfway through I stopped really following and just let it bounce.

### I was confused
- **Time of day.** Page 2, panel 4 is "late morning" at the rim, where he says "One day, I'm leaving." Page 3 is "late afternoon at the same overlook." Has he been sitting there all day? I'd have read it as one continuous scene and not noticed the light changed, and then wondered why he says the same kind of thing twice.
- **Page 3, panel 3.** He goes from "*One day*, I'm leaving" on page 2 to Ada saying "you're planning to leave *before tomorrow*." When did "one day" turn into tonight? How does she know? Is he actually running tonight? This is the biggest thing B tells me, and I only half caught it inside a run of quips.
- **"Where you were all night?" / "Working." / "before dawn."** I couldn't tell if this matters (is he hiding something?) or if it's just banter. It was confusing and it didn't make me curious. I let it go.
- **Page 3, panel 4.** "Then don't spend them proving he was right about people leaving." Who is "he"? The dad? Why would the dad be right about people leaving? Who left? B never mentions a mother, so I had nothing to hook this onto. I gave up on it.
- **"Paying for what he did."** What did he do? A at least told me he "lost everything." B gives me nothing.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First appears | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Oasis / Halyard / Keel | p1 caption | Yes, roughly. The caption plus the picture tells me which city is which. |
| Alpha / white-and-amber nodes | p1 | Never named. It's "the scanner thing." |
| "Debt Transfer Day" | p2 screen | Sort of. It sounds like a thing everyone knows about. I don't know if everyone gets one or just him. |
| Adrian Phantum | p2 screen | Assumed dad. Never said. |
| The casino chip with the equation | p2 p3 | Not explained. |
| The sealed mine | p2 p4 (art), p3 p4 | It's pointed at, not explained. This one felt deliberate and I was fine with it. |
| "People leaving" / who left | p3 p4 | Never. |
| "The story" | p3 p4 | Implied: that he left on purpose. |

### Lines I read twice
- "You look expensive." (p3 p1) Got it the second time: the debt.
- "It's the part where you pretend it isn't." (p3 p3)
- "Then don't spend them proving he was right about people leaving." (p3 p4) I gave up on this one.
- "I think everybody's been very sure of a story nobody can show you." (p3 p4) I got it on the second read, but it's a sentence you have to untangle.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Alex is clear: dry and deflecting.
- Ada is more of a person than in A. She needles him, she knows his habits, and she watches him instead of the view. But she and Alex both talk in the same clever-comeback rhythm, so on page 3 they started to sound like one voice doing both sides. "Tea's free." / "Nothing's free." / "You say that like you invented debt." / "I only inherited it." It's a bit too polished. Honestly, this is the kind of back-and-forth my friends would call AI-sounding.
- I still don't know what she is to him. She feels like an old friend, maybe more. At least in B that felt like something to find out instead of a gap.
- The workers in the queue are background, but they did a job.

### I felt something
- Page 2, panel 3: the worker looking away. That was the strongest moment for me in either version.
- Page 3, panel 4, "The chip stops turning": I noticed the beat when he got hit by what she said. Small, but it landed.

### I predicted
- Same as A: dad didn't just run, and the chip is a clue. Plus a new one: something happened in the sealed mine and the dad is tied to it. And Alex is going to try to leave tonight, but Ada's question will send him into the mine instead.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A kid who inherits his dad's debt on his 17th birthday is about to run, until his friend makes him wonder whether his dad's disappearance has something to do with the sealed mine.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 3, panel 3, the "where were you all night / before dawn / before tomorrow" exchange. It's the stretch where I was reading lines and not following a scene.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
More than with A, a bit. "What if they're wrong?" is the same question, but the look at the sealed mine gives it a direction, and "before tomorrow" gives it a clock. I'm not desperate, because I still don't care about the dad himself. But I'd turn the page to see if Alex runs tonight. Part of the last page lost me, though ("proving he was right about people leaving"), so I came out of it slightly fuzzy instead of sharp.

---

## Which one I would keep reading, and the moment that decided it
B, narrowly, with complaints. The deciding moment was **B, page 2, panel 3**: the worker who glances at Alex's balance and looks away. Nothing on A's page 2 made me feel the debt in front of other people like that. The sealed-mine glance at the end of B also gave me somewhere to look. Against that, A is faster, cleaner and easier to follow on one read, and I never got lost in it. B's page 3 lost me twice. A lost me with one fake line about his mother. If I'm being honest, the hook in both is the same scanner screen. A delivers it clean and then goes flat. B delivers it with a witness and then gets too clever.

## One-sentence aftertaste of each
- **A:** A great debt screen, followed by a friend who reads out the backstory.
- **B:** A kid embarrassed in a queue and a sealed door worth wondering about, buried under some dialogue that's too pleased with itself.

reasoning_details.text:
I'll read through as a skeptical teen giving blunt, specific first impressions, starting with Version A's opening splash page where the visual of three cities and a narrowing pipe immediately communicates the rich-top/poor-bottom class divide.

Page 2 has a solid cocky exchange ("Then don't approve it"), and the debt display with 418,607 credits and 28.7 years is the real hook of the scene — though "Keep it locked, I might run" reads a bit confusingly since it's unclear whether the gate is restricting him from leaving work or leaving the city entirely. Page 3's chip reveal plays nicely ambiguous between inheritance and debt, though Ada's line about the balance mostly just restates what we already saw on-page.

The "getting out of Keel, Ada, before I end up like him" line introduces the town name and hints "him" is a father figure, but Ada's follow-up about the mother leaving feels like forced exposition rather than natural dialogue, and her relationship to the protagonist is never established. The gambling chip with an equation is intriguing and suggests the dad lost everything gambling, but the closing line "What if the official story is wrong?" is a fairly generic hook — the debt reveal does more work to make me want to turn the page than that final question does.

Comparing to version B, the same splash page labels the three locations top-to-bottom which helps with mapping names to places, but the supervisor's dialogue feels slightly padded. The debt transfer scene lands harder here though — showing other workers' modest balances next to Alex's huge one, with everyone looking away, is a stronger visual gut-punch than a line of dialogue would be.

There's a timeline snag though: Ada says the shift ended before dawn, but the pit rim scene is tagged "late morning" and then recurs "late afternoon at the same overlook" — so is he sitting there the whole day, or is this a different visit? The lighting shift in the art suggests the latter, but without clear lettering a reader could easily read it as one continuous scene. It's a minor continuity wrinkle, but combined with his "one day, I'm leaving" line escalating into Ada's "planning to leave before tomorrow," the pacing of that escalation needs the timeline to be unambiguous.

The banter also strains plausibility — Ada apparently knows about the debt and that it's transfer day, which hasn't been established on-page, so the "you look expensive"/"twenty-eight-year warranty" exchange reads clever but unearned. Some lines land ("it's the part where you pretend it isn't") while others get murky, especially "don't spend them proving he was right about people leaving" — the "he" is ambiguous since Mom is never mentioned, so it's unclear if Dad is being referenced or someone else. The closing beat with Ada looking at the sealed mine entrance and wondering "what if they're wrong?" feels intriguing and worth following up on.

In script B, the father is never explicitly named, and "paying for what he did" raises a question that never gets answered — what exactly did he do? Script A, by contrast, clarifies that the mother left and everything was lost, giving more grounding information.

Comparing the two Alexes, both read as dry and similar in voice. Ada functions more as exposition in A, while in B she's sharper and more needling, giving her a stronger personality, though it also makes her sound like another quipper rather than a distinct voice. The supervisor and guard characters stay indistinct in both, which is fine.

Weighing which script I'd keep reading, I lean toward B because the workers glancing away and Ada's look toward the sealed mine give the mystery a physical anchor, even though some of the dialogue on page three lost me. A moves faster and reads more clearly, though the mother line felt a bit inauthentic. I think the deciding moment is that worker-glance beat or the mine look in B — I'm leaning toward picking that as the throughline.

Weighing it again, I'll go with B, though narrowly and with some reservations. For what to highlight: in A, it's Ada's mother line on page three (worth noting with some skepticism, not dismissing it); in B, it's the "where were you all night" exchange on page three. Now I'm ready to write this up.
